# Division of labour and specialisation (`division_of_labour`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by price_mechanism_supply_demand
- Core idea: Splitting a job into simple steps, each done all day by one person, multiplies output: practice makes each worker fast, no time is lost changing tasks and tools, and a simple repeated motion is easy to give to a machine. Smith's pin workshop: ten workers splitting 18 operations made about 48,000 pins a day, where each alone might make twenty. The limit is the size of the market: it pays only where goods can be sold in large numbers, so roads, canals and free trade widen it. Babbage added that skilled, highly paid workers can then be kept for the skilled steps alone.
- Pitfalls:
  - Specialising production before there is a market for the output: the goods pile up unsold
  - Ignoring the human cost: Smith himself warned that endlessly repeating one motion makes a worker 'as stupid and ignorant as it is possible'
  - Forgetting coordination: one missing step or sick worker stops the whole line
  - Treating it as modern: Ur III textile workshops, Han lacquer workshops and the Venetian Arsenal practised it
  - Confusing it with hereditary assignment of trades by birth, which blocks people from moving to where they are most productive
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2100–2000 BC – Ur III state textile workshops employ thousands of women weavers in specialised teams; greece: c. 370 BC – Xenophon (Cyropaedia VIII.2.5) notes that in large cities one man makes only men's shoes and another only women's, and the work is better for it; Plato, Republic II; china: 1st c. BC–1st c. AD – Han lacquer cups inscribed with the names of six or more specialised craftsmen and supervisors; Qin standardised crossbow parts; islamic: 1377 – Ibn Khaldun (Muqaddimah) explains that cooperation and specialisation produce far more than any person needs, the basis of urban wealth; india: occupational castes (jati) fix trades by birth, a specialisation by heredity rather than choice; europe: 15th–16th c. – the Venetian Arsenal fits out galleys on an assembly line; 1776 Smith; 1832 Babbage
- Read:
  - Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776), book I ch. 1–3
  - Charles Babbage, On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures (1832)
  - Ibn Khaldun, Muqaddimah (1377)
